name: Kanju
readall_conflicts: No source opened states Kaantju word stress, so there is nothing to conflict. Among the sister varieties in the same volume the descriptions differ in detail: Thompson (Kuuku-Ya'u, p.216) gives last long vowel, else first vowel (weight-sensitive), while O'Grady (Umpila, p.60ff, snippet) says 'Stress in Umpila falls on the first syllable of a word. If the first vowel (V1)..' (the continuation was not captured, so whether O'Grady also allows long-vowel attraction is unknown). Thompson 1988 gives the same long-vowel rule for both Kuuku Ya'u and Umpila. Verstraete et al. 2025 (Australian Journal of Linguistics, embargoed, not opened) asks whether Eastern Middle Paman medial consonant lengthening reflects syllable position or lexical stress, which suggests the stress analysis of this cluster is still contested.

sources.citation: Thompson, David A. 1988. Lockhart River "Sand Beach" Language: An Outline of Kuuku Ya'u and Umpila. Work Papers of SIL-AAIB, Series A Vol. 11. Darwin: SIL. (Rosetta Project excerpts on archive.org tagged 'kbe'/'Kanju': detail-2 = §1.1, §1.3; phon-2 = §2, §2.1; ortho-1 = §7 pp.62-63; morsyn-2 = §3; vertxt-1 = §6)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §7.2.4 p.63 (Kuuku Ya'u and Umpila, NOT Kaantju): 'In words with no long vowels the first vowel is stressed, e.g. táwura. In words with long vowels the the last long vowel is stressed, e.g. páala, muumáanya, pitáanchi, tawuráalu'; §7.2.3: in words with no long vowel the first syllable is stressed and the next consonant is lengthened (pama -> pámma). §1.1/§1.3 explicitly scope the description to the two coastal dialects and call Kaantju 'the inland dialect'; no Kaantju data given. The 'more detail' §2.4 p.6 is not in any excerpt.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter & Ken Hale. 2021. Linguistic Organisation and Native Title: The Wik Case, Australia. Canberra: ANU Press (open access). Ch.6 Hale, 'Wik Subgroup lexical history' pp.133-176; ch.7 Hale, 'Wik Subgroup grammatical history' pp.177-220 (the two Glottolog 'overview' refs for kanj1260)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Kaanju stress. Hale treats 'Kaanju-Ya'u-Umpila (Ka, Ya)' as one eastern Middle Paman language (language list item 30 Ka: Kaanju, 30' Ya: Kuuku Ya'u-Umpila); ch.7 pp.202-203 gives Kaanju example sentences from Hale's 1960 notes for dependent pronominals only. Stress remarks in the book concern Wik-Me'nh/Wik-Ngathan (unstressed vowel reduction; primary word stress on first syllable, fn.5 p.182).

sources.note: Comparative-historical phonology; the classic source on Middle Paman medial-consonant lengthening / stress that the 2025 article revisits. Hale had Kaantju field data (1960) and treats Kaanju-Ya'u-Umpila as one language, so any stress generalisation there would be the earliest statement bearing on Kaantju. AIATSIS annotation says its examples are Wik, so Kaantju content is uncertain.
